claim: Evoked responses of arousal systems during decisions are reported by rapid dilations of the pupil.
source: In previous work in humans, we found that evoked responses of arousal systems during decisions are reported by rapid dilations of the pupil and track a suppression of biases in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence (de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (de Gee et al., 2017).

claim: Rapid pupil dilations during decisions track a suppression of biases in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence.
source: In previous work in humans, we found that evoked responses of arousal systems during decisions are reported by rapid dilations of the pupil and track a suppression of biases in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence (de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (de Gee et al., 2017).

claim: Arousal-related suppression in decision bias acts on both conservative and liberal biases.
source: Here, we show that this arousal-related suppression in decision bias acts on both conservative and liberal biases, and generalizes from humans to mice, and from perceptual to memory-based decisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 1-3 showing bias suppression across different conditions.

claim: Arousal-related suppression in decision bias generalizes from humans to mice.
source: Here, we show that this arousal-related suppression in decision bias acts on both conservative and liberal biases, and generalizes from humans to mice, and from perceptual to memory-based decisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from both human and mouse experiments presented in Figure 1.

claim: Arousal-related suppression in decision bias generalizes from perceptual to memory-based decisions.
source: Here, we show that this arousal-related suppression in decision bias acts on both conservative and liberal biases, and generalizes from humans to mice, and from perceptual to memory-based decisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from both perceptual (Figures 1-2) and memory-based (Figure 3) decision tasks.

claim: In challenging sound-detection tasks, the impact of spontaneous or experimentally induced choice biases was reduced under high phasic arousal.
source: In challenging sound-detection tasks, the impact of spontaneous or experimentally induced choice biases was reduced under high phasic arousal.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing reduced bias in high pupil response bins.

claim: Bias suppression occurred when evidence was drawn from memory.
source: Similar bias suppression occurred when evidence was drawn from memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the picture recognition task presented in Figure 3.

claim: All behavioral effects were explained by reduced evidence accumulation biases.
source: All of these behavioral effects were explained by reduced evidence accumulation biases.
evidence: The claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results presented in Figure 4.

claim: The global arousal state of the brain changes from moment to moment.
source: The global arousal state of the brain changes from moment to moment (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Global state changes are controlled in large part by modulatory neurotransmitters that are released from subcortical nuclei such as the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) and the cholinergic basal forebrain.
source: These global state changes are controlled in large part by modulatory neurotransmitters that are released from subcortical nuclei such as the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) and the cholinergic basal forebrain.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about arousal systems.

claim: Release of neuromodulators can profoundly change the operating mode of target cortical circuits.
source: Release of these neuromodulators can profoundly change the operating mode of target cortical circuits (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Froemke, 2015; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Lee and Dan, 2012; Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Arousal systems are phasically recruited during elementary decisions, in relation to computational variables such as uncertainty about making the correct choice and surprise about decision outcome.
source: These same arousal systems are phasically recruited during elementary decisions, in relation to computational variables such as uncertainty about making the correct choice and surprise about decision outcome (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Colizoli et al., 2018; Dayan and Yu, 2006; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Lak et al., 2017; Nassar et al., 2012; Parikh et al., 2007; Urai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Most decisions are based on a protracted accumulation of decision-relevant evidence.
source: Most decisions – including judgments about weak sensory signals in noise – are based on a protracted accumulation of decision-relevant evidence (Shadlen and Kiani, 2013) implemented in a distributed network of brain regions (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on decision-making.

claim: In perceptual decisions, noise-corrupted decision evidence is encoded in sensory cortex, and downstream regions of association and motor cortices accumulate the fluctuating sensory response over time into a decision variable that forms the basis of behavioral choice.
source: In perceptual decisions, noise-corrupted decision evidence is encoded in sensory cortex, and downstream regions of association and motor cortices accumulate the fluctuating sensory response over time into a decision variable that forms the basis of behavioral choice (Bogacz et al., 2006; Shadlen and Kiani, 2013; Siegel et al., 2011; Wang, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on perceptual decision-making.

claim: All brain regions involved in decision-making are impacted by the brain's arousal systems.
source: All of these brain regions are impacted by the brain's arousal systems.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about arousal system projections.

claim: Rapid pupil dilations during perceptual decisions report evoked responses in specific neuromodulatory (brainstem) nuclei controlling arousal, including the noradrenergic LC.
source: We found that rapid pupil dilations during perceptual decisions report evoked responses in specific neuromodulatory (brainstem) nuclei controlling arousal, including the noradrenergic LC.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors combining fMRI, pupillometry and behavioral modeling.

claim: Pupil responses track a suppression of pre-existing biases in the accumulation of perceptual evidence.
source: We also showed that those same pupil responses track a suppression of pre-existing biases in the accumulation of perceptual evidence.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (de Gee et al., 2017).

claim: In perceptual detection tasks, spontaneously emerging 'conservative' biases (towards reporting the absence of a target signal) were reduced under large phasic arousal.
source: Specifically, in perceptual detection tasks, spontaneously emerging 'conservative' biases (towards reporting the absence of a target signal) were reduced under large phasic arousal.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (de Gee et al., 2017).

claim: Rodents (rats) can accumulate perceptual evidence in a similar fashion to that in humans.
source: Indeed, rodents (rats) can accumulate perceptual evidence in a similar fashion to that in humans (Brunton et al., 2013), their arousal systems are organized homologously with those of humans (Amaral and Sinnamon, 1977; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003), and pupil dilation reports arousal also in rodents (McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brunton et al., 2013.

claim: Rodent arousal systems are organized homologously with those of humans.
source: Indeed, rodents (rats) can accumulate perceptual evidence in a similar fashion to that in humans (Brunton et al., 2013), their arousal systems are organized homologously with those of humans (Amaral and Sinnamon, 1977; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003), and pupil dilation reports arousal also in rodents (McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amaral and Sinnamon, 1977; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003.

claim: Pupil dilation reports arousal in rodents.
source: Indeed, rodents (rats) can accumulate perceptual evidence in a similar fashion to that in humans (Brunton et al., 2013), their arousal systems are organized homologously with those of humans (Amaral and Sinnamon, 1977; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003), and pupil dilation reports arousal also in rodents (McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015.

claim: Pupil responses occurred as early as 40 ms after trial onset in mice.
source: Pupil responses occurred as early as 40 ms after trial onset in mice (Figure 1C, top), and from 240 ms after trial onset in humans (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pupil responses occurred from 240 ms after trial onset in humans.
source: Pupil responses occurred as early as 40 ms after trial onset in mice (Figure 1C, top), and from 240 ms after trial onset in humans (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both mice and humans had an overall conservative choice bias, often failing to report the signal tones.
source: Both mice and humans had an overall conservative choice bias, often failing to report the signal tones (Figure 1D; bias computed after collapsing across signal loudness levels; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,H and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: In both species, conservative bias was significantly reduced in trials characterized by large pupil responses.
source: In both species, this conservative bias was significantly reduced in trials characterized by large pupil responses (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mice were faster and more sensitive in trials that were characterized by large pupil responses.
source: Mice were faster and more sensitive in trials that were characterized by large pupil responses, but this relationship did not generalize to humans (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The relationship between large pupil responses and faster, more sensitive performance did not generalize from mice to humans.
source: Mice were faster and more sensitive in trials that were characterized by large pupil responses, but this relationship did not generalize to humans (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pupil responses in the go/no-go and yes/no tasks were correlated across participants, for both yes and no choices.
source: We found that pupil responses in the go/no-go and yes/no tasks were correlated across participants, for both yes and no choices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pupil response in both tasks primarily reflected decision processing rather than motor preparation or execution.
source: This result indicates that pupil response in both tasks primarily reflected decision processing rather than motor preparation or execution.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between pupil responses in go/no-go and yes/no tasks.

claim: Subjects developed a conservative bias in the rare signal condition and a liberal bias in the frequent signal condition.
source: As expected (Green and Swets, 1966), subjects developed a conservative bias in the rare signal condition and a liberal bias in the frequent signal condition (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with signal detection theory.

claim: Pupil response predicted a change in choice biases towards neutral for both rare and frequent block types.
source: Importantly, pupil response predicted a change in choice biases towards neutral for both block types (performed within the same experimental session) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Subjects' overall biases varied from strongly liberal to strongly conservative across the 54 individuals in the picture recognition task.
source: Subjects' overall biases (irrespective of pupil response) varied from strongly liberal to strongly conservative across the 54 individuals (Figure 3C, x-axis and colors).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Subjects with the strongest overall biases, whether liberal or conservative, exhibited the strongest pupil-linked shift towards neutral bias.
source: Indeed, we observed a robust relationship between subjects' overall choice bias, and the pupil-linked shift in that bias: subjects with the strongest overall biases, whether liberal or conservative, exhibited the strongest pupil-linked shift towards neutral bias (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The absolute value of the bias was significantly reduced towards 0 in high-pupil bins.
source: Correspondingly, the absolute value of the of the bias, measuring the magnitude of bias irrespective of sign, was significantly reduced towards 0 in high-pupil bins (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D (note: this appears to be a typo in the manuscript, should be Figure 3D).

claim: The individual pupil-linked changes in drift bias, but not in starting point, strongly correlated with the corresponding changes in the overt behavioral biases.
source: More importantly, the individual pupil-linked changes in drift bias, but not in starting point, strongly correlated with the corresponding changes in the overt behavioral biases (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pupil responses predicted linear shifts in drift bias in all data sets.
source: In line with the results described above, pupil responses predicted linear shifts in drift bias in all data sets (Figure 4C), but not (consistently) in starting point (for yes/no data; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pupil responses did not consistently predict shifts in starting point across data sets.
source: In line with the results described above, pupil responses predicted linear shifts in drift bias in all data sets (Figure 4C), but not (consistently) in starting point (for yes/no data; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The pupil-linked behavioral effects in all data sets were consistent with a phasic arousal-dependent, selective reduction in the bias of the evidence accumulation process.
source: In summary, the pupil-linked behavioral effects in all of the data sets analyzed here were consistent with a phasic arousal-dependent, selective reduction in the bias of the evidence accumulation process that underlies the decisions assessed here.
evidence: The claim is supported by the drift diffusion modeling results across all datasets.

claim: Pupil dilation exhibited no consistent association with changes of drift rate across data sets.
source: Correspondingly, pupil dilation also exhibited no consistent (across data sets) association with changes of drift rate (measure of sensitivity), and no association with boundary separation (measure of response caution) or non-decision time (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Pupil dilation exhibited no association with boundary separation or non-decision time.
source: Correspondingly, pupil dilation also exhibited no consistent (across data sets) association with changes of drift rate (measure of sensitivity), and no association with boundary separation (measure of response caution) or non-decision time (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: When drift bias was allowed to vary with condition, the model was able to recover the true drift rate variability of the generative process.
source: When we allowed drift bias to vary with condition (as we did in our pupil-dependent model fits above), we were actually able to recover the true drift rate variability of the generative process (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When drift bias was forced to be the same for both conditions, drift rate variability was overestimated.
source: But when we forced the drift bias to be the same for both conditions, drift rate variability was overestimated (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The additional ('apparent') component of drift rate variability increased monotonically with the disparity of drift biases between both conditions.
source: This additional ('apparent') component of drift rate variability increased monotonically with the disparity of drift biases between both conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A significant fraction of choice variability does not originate from noise within the evidence accumulation machinery itself, but rather from dynamic, arousal-linked variations in evidence accumulation bias.
source: Thus, a significant fraction of choice variability does not originate from noise within the evidence accumulation machinery itself, but rather from dynamic, arousal-linked variations in evidence accumulation bias.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the simulation results showing that drift bias variations appear as drift rate variability.

claim: The model with collapsing bounds produced only negligible pupil-linked variations in choice bias.
source: The model with collapsing bounds produced only negligible pupil-linked variations in choice bias (Figure 6B), contrary to what we observed in all data sets (Figures 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In each data set, the residuals of the drift bias model were smallest, indicating that this model best captured the pupil-dependent variation in overt choice bias.
source: In each data set, the residuals of the drift bias model were smallest (Figure 6C), indicating that this model best captured the pupil-dependent variation in overt choice bias.
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Changes in drift bias, but in neither starting point nor decision urgency, implement the pupil-linked shifts in choice bias.
source: Taken together, all of our modeling efforts converged on the conclusion that changes in drift bias, but in neither starting point nor decision urgency (combined with a pre-existing starting point bias), implement the pupil-linked shifts in choice bias.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive modeling results across all datasets.

claim: There was a non-monotonic association between baseline pupil diameter and decision bias in mice.
source: First, there was a non-monotonic association between baseline pupil diameter and decision bias in mice (McGinley et al., 2015a), in contrast to the monotonic pattern that we observed here for phasic arousal in the same data set (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McGinley et al., 2015a and comparison with current results.

claim: Pupil responses exhibited a negligible (go/no-go data sets) or weak (yes/no data sets) correlation with the preceding baseline diameter.
source: Second, pupil responses exhibited a negligible (go/no-go data sets) or weak (yes/no data sets) correlation with the preceding baseline diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C); in all cases, these correlations are substantially smaller than those for conventional baseline-corrected pupil response amplitudes (de Gee et al., 2014; Gilzenrat et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The reduction in choice bias linked to pupil responses reflects genuine correlates of phasic arousal, and not of the slowly varying, baseline arousal state.
source: In summary, the reduction in choice bias linked to pupil responses reported here reflects genuine correlates of phasic arousal, and not of the slowly varying, baseline arousal state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analyses showing weak correlations between pupil responses and baseline pupil size.

claim: Phasic arousal suppresses biases in the accumulation of evidence leading up to a choice, a function that generalizes across species (humans and mice) and domains of decision-making (from perceptual to memory-based).
source: Our results are in consistent with the idea that phasic arousal suppresses biases in the accumulation of evidence leading up to a choice, a function that generalizes across species (humans and mice) and domains of decision-making (from perceptual to memory-based).
evidence: The claim is supported by the comprehensive results across all experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Pupil diameter closely tracks several established measures of cortical arousal state.
source: Indeed, recent work has shown that pupil diameter closely tracks several established measures of cortical arousal state (Larsen and Waters, 2018; McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Changes in pupil diameter have been associated with locus coeruleus (LC) activity in humans, monkeys, and mice.
source: Changes in pupil diameter have been associated with locus coeruleus (LC) activity in humans (de Gee et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2014), monkeys (Joshi et al., 2016; Varazzani et al., 2015), and mice (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Liu et al., 2017; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations across species.

claim: Some studies found unique contributions to pupil size in other subcortical regions, such as the cholinergic basal forebrain and dopaminergic midbrain, and the superior and inferior colliculi.
source: However, some (of these) studies also found unique contributions to pupil size in other subcortical regions, such as the cholinergic basal forebrain and dopaminergic midbrain, and the superior and inferior colliculi (de Gee et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2016; Mridha et al., 2019; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: During sound localization in a dynamic environment, phasic arousal tracks a reduced influence of prior expectations on perception.
source: Similarly, during sound localization in a dynamic environment, phasic arousal tracks a reduced influence of prior expectations on perception (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krishnamurthy et al., 2017.

claim: Phasic arousal reflects perceptual decision uncertainty in the current trial and a reduction of choice repetition bias in the next trial.
source: In this case, phasic arousal reflects perceptual decision uncertainty in the current trial and a reduction of choice repetition bias in the next trial (Urai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Urai et al., 2017.

claim: The mice's behavioral performance was most rapid and accurate, and the least biased, at intermediate levels of 'tonic' arousal (medium baseline pupil size).
source: A previous report on that data set showed that the mice's behavioral performance was most rapid and accurate, and the least biased, at intermediate levels of 'tonic' arousal (medium baseline pupil size) (McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McGinley et al., 2015a.

claim: The behavioral performance of the mice was linearly related to phasic arousal, with the most rapid and accurate and the least biased choices being associated with the most rapid phasic arousal responses.
source: By contrast, we show here that the behavioral performance of the mice was linearly related to phasic arousal, with the most rapid and accurate and the least biased choices being associated with the most rapid phasic arousal responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript for mice.

claim: Rapid dilations of the pupil (phasic arousal) are more tightly associated with phasic activity in noradrenergic axons, whereas slow changes in pupil (tonic arousal) are accompanied by sustained activity in cholinergic axons.
source: Indeed, rapid dilations of the pupil (phasic arousal) are more tightly associated with phasic activity in noradrenergic axons, whereas slow changes in pupil (tonic arousal) are accompanied by sustained activity in cholinergic axons (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reimer et al., 2016.

claim: Optical stimulation of LC inputs to anterior cingulate cortex caused rats to abandon strategic counter prediction in favor of stochastic choice in a competitive game.
source: First, optical stimulation of LC inputs to anterior cingulate cortex caused rats to abandon strategic counter prediction in favor of stochastic choice in a competitive game (Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tervo et al., 2014.

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of the LC in rats performing a patch-leaving task increased decision noise and subsequent exploration.
source: Second, chemogenetic stimulation of the LC in rats performing a patch-leaving task increased decision noise and subsequent exploration (Kane et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kane et al., 2017.

claim: Pharmacologically reducing central NA levels in monkeys performing an operant effort exertion task parametrically increased choice consistency.
source: Third, pharmacologically reducing central NA levels in monkeys performing an operant effort exertion task parametrically increased choice consistency (Jahn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jahn et al., 2018.

claim: Pharmacologically increasing central tonic NA levels in human subjects boosted the rate of alternations in a bistable visual input and long-range correlations in brain activity.
source: Finally, pharmacologically increasing central tonic NA levels in human subjects boosted the rate of alternations in a bistable visual input and long-range correlations in brain activity (Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pfeffer et al., 2018.

claim: Phasic arousal affected evidence accumulation (suppressing biases therein), but not non-decision time.
source: In contrast to this prediction, we found in all our datasets that phasic arousal affected evidence accumulation (suppressing biases therein), but not non-decision time.
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling results across all datasets.

claim: Phasic arousal has an important role in evidence accumulation, ruling out any purely post-decisional account.
source: Yet, our results clearly establish an important role of phasic arousal in evidence accumulation, ruling out any purely post-decisional account.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the modeling results showing effects on drift bias but not non-decision time.
